newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French officials call for credible euro.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French officials call for credible euro.

text.p: Europe should aim for a single currency that is as stable and credible as possible to ensure a future European monetary union benefits from low interest rates, senior French finance officials said on Wednesday.
"The future credibility of the euro...is, I remind you, a condition for the lowest possible interest rates," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said.

This credibility would be underpinned by a budget discipline pact proposed by Germany to ensure members of economic and monetary union (EMU) do not run up big deficits after the launch of the euro in 1999, he told a business conference.

The Bank of France's deputy governor, Herve Hannoun, a staunch defender of currency stability for the French franc, said the euro must be a solid currency. "The euro must be as solid and credible as the franc," he said.
"This is naturally a factor which allows one to think that the euro zone will be a zone with relatively low interest rates," he said.

Their comments were the latest sally in a debate in France on exchange rates, which has tapped into a long-standing split in policy towards the franc and fuelled talk of a rift between France and Germany over monetary policies.
At issue is what French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has called the chronic undervaluation of the dollar.

According to some, France needs action now to depreciate the franc against the dollar. Unless it gets German backing for concerted action to push the dollar higher -- by lowering European interest rates -- it should, if necessary, plump for a devaluation of the franc against the mark, they say.
The government has insisted there is no need to change the franc-mark rate -- a comment reiterated on Wednesday by Arthuis.

He also said he hoped the switch to the euro would be at around 6.50 francs -- in line with a current rate of 6.53 francs per European currency unit (Ecu), for which the euro will be exchanged one-for-one.
Some economists believe there is nonetheless support in the government for a softer monetary policy than sought by Germany, both before and after the launch of the euro.
A weakening of European currencies against the dollar would boost European exports and revive economic growth.

Hannoun declined to comment on the debate on the franc, but said since no one could predict the level of the dollar at the launch of the euro, the question of the euro-dollar rate was not an issue right now. "It does not arise immediately," he said.
Arthuis said the best rate for a currency was one that allowed the lowest possible interest rates.

The Bank of France has long insisted that its policy of keeping the franc stable against the mark has all but erased the risk premium France had to pay on its borrowings and brought the country low long and short-term interest rates.
Opponents, however, blame record unemployment and sluggish growth, at least partly, on that policy.
It is a battle that has divided France for more than a decade, and looks set to continue with monetary union.
On one side are those who argue the future European Central Bank must make the euro as stable as possible to guarantee low interest rates for the euro zone.

They say that as the currency gains credibility, the euro will become a rival reserve currency to the dollar, making it hard for the United States to maintain a weak currency while also enjoying low interest rates.
On the other side are those who say that the need to combat unemployment now rules out this longer-term scenario.

Some believe that President Jacques Chirac may be caught in the middle. Until now he has backed the monetary and fiscal orthodoxy favoured by the Bank of France, but he is also under pressure from some politicians in his own party for a change of tack. So far he has shown no signs of wavering.
